log.reply:
# Practitioner Academy Proposal

**Prepared for:** Dana Whitfield, General Counsel, Tamarack Instruments
**Program:** Practitioner Academy, AI Governance Academy
**Basis:** Discovery call notes of 6 October 2026 with Dana Whitfield, Ravi Okafor and Ingrid Solberg

## 1. Situation Summary

Tamarack Instruments designs and manufactures laboratory measurement instruments. It is headquartered in the Netherlands and operates in the Netherlands, Germany and the United States, with about 1,100 staff. The Client's AI estate has three stages:

- A customer service chatbot is deployed on the support portal.
- AI visual inspection is being piloted on the German production line.
- AI sales forecasting is planned for next year.

The Client describes its AI maturity as Piloting and names the EU AI Act and GDPR as regulatory drivers. An internal audit finding in June 2026 recorded that no inventory of AI systems exists. ISO/IEC 42001 work is expected to start next year, with the start date not yet fixed.

Your stated objective is clear: "I want governance in place before visual inspection goes into production in Q2 2027." Three constraints shape the work:

- Budget is approved up to US$80,000 this fiscal year.
- Customer data must stay in the EU.
- The German works council is consulted before anything touches production staff.

The Client names ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO 9001 as incumbent frameworks. This proposal does not assume any register, process, control or record from those systems. Whether participants hold related documents they can bring is `Unknown`.

## 2. Why Hands-On Practitioner Capability Fits Now

The audit finding, the Q2 2027 production target and next year's ISO/IEC 42001 start point to the same need. The Client needs people who can build and maintain governance artifacts, not only people who have read about them.

The Practitioner Academy has participants work directly in two open repositories:

- GRC Workbook (https://github.com/rolldabones/grc-workbook)
- Slow AI Kitchen (https://github.com/rolldabones/slow-ai-kitchen)

Participants use their own AI systems as the working material. They leave with started artifacts and a clear sense of where each one lives. The program is anchored in three principles: Slow AI, Informed Intent, Final Liability rests with the Human.

The participant group combines legal, security, quality, data, plant and audit perspectives:

- General Counsel
- CISO
- Head of Quality
- Head of Data
- German plant manager
- Two internal auditors

This lets each artifact be drafted and challenged by the functions that will later rely on it.

## 3. Worked Examples

Three of the Client's use cases run through both days:

1. **AI visual inspection (piloting).** This is the system tied directly to your Q2 2027 objective. It also exercises the works council constraint.
2. **Customer service chatbot (deployed).** As the one system already in use, it tests inventory, oversight and evidence on a live system. It also exercises the EU data residency constraint.
3. **AI sales forecasting (planned).** This system shows how a system is classified and governed before it is built, which is the intake discipline an inventory needs to stay current.

Each system's classification under the EU AI Act is an output of the exercises, not a premise of this proposal.

## 4. Curriculum Spine and Exercises

The program runs over two days, live and virtual. Each day has four 90-minute working sessions.

### Day 1: GRC Workbook (https://github.com/rolldabones/grc-workbook)

| Session | Exercise | Workbook module | Artifact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Governance structures | Map decision rights across the three use cases. Named owners not confirmed in the room are recorded as `Unknown` for the Client to complete. | Governance structures module | Draft AI governance roles and decision rights map |
| 2. AI system inventories and classification | Enter the chatbot, visual inspection pilot and planned forecasting system, with a draft classification for each. This responds directly to the June 2026 finding. | Inventory and classification module | Started AI system inventory |
| 3. Risk and impact assessments | Assess the visual inspection pilot and the chatbot. | Risk and impact assessment module | Draft risk register entries |
| 4. Policies and operating procedures | Draft a pre-production gate procedure for AI systems. It includes an EU data residency check and a works council consultation step wherever a system could touch production staff. | Policies and operating procedures module | Draft operating procedure |

Session 1 also includes the teaching fable *The Turtle and the Phoenix*, told from the facilitation kit (https://github.com/rolldabones/AI-Governance-Academy/blob/main/the-turtle-and-the-phoenix.md). Its purpose is to seat the doctrine before the instruments arrive on Day 2. The kit's handle map links the story to the workbook modules used through Day 1.

### Day 2: Slow AI Kitchen (https://github.com/rolldabones/slow-ai-kitchen) plus assurance

| Session | Exercise | Kitchen pattern or reference | Artifact |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5. Governed prompting | Build a governed prompt for chatbot support responses using synthetic support tickets. No real customer data enters the exercise. | Governed prompting pattern | Governed prompt card |
| 6. Practical AI workflow design | Design two workflows: (a) the visual inspection pilot-to-production decision, using synthetic defect descriptions with no production images or staff data, and (b) chatbot escalation to a human agent. | Workflow design pattern | Two governed workflows |
| 7. Human oversight and accountability | Define human decision and override points for inspection rejects and chatbot escalations. | Human oversight pattern | Oversight and accountability map |
| 8. Evidence collection and audit readiness | Define the evidence each Day 1 and Day 2 artifact must produce. Set acceptance criteria using The Definition of Done (https://github.com/rolldabones/definition-of-done). Note how results report upward using AI Governance for Boards (https://github.com/rolldabones/ai-governance-for-boards). | Evidence and audit readiness module, The Definition of Done | Evidence plan and audit readiness checklist |

Exact repository file names for each module and pattern will be confirmed in the pre-work packet.

## 5. Deliverables

Participants leave with:

- A started AI system inventory covering the three named systems
- Draft risk register entries for the visual inspection pilot and the chatbot
- At least two governed workflows
- A decision rights map
- A pre-production gate procedure
- A governed prompt card
- An oversight and accountability map
- An evidence plan

All artifacts are drafts for the Client to complete and approve. The program does not certify the Client or predict the outcome of any audit, including future ISO/IEC 42001 work.

## 6. Logistics and Price

- **Format:** Live virtual, two days, four 90-minute working sessions per day.
- **Price:** US$12,500, within the stated budget of up to US$80,000 this fiscal year.
- **Participants:** The seven roles listed in Section 2.
- **Participant locations and session times:** `Unknown`, to be agreed.
- **Dates:** `Unknown`. We recommend a date that leaves time to finish the drafted artifacts before the Q2 2027 production target.
- **Data handling:** Exercises use sanitized and synthetic analogs only. No customer data or production staff data is required.

## 7. Next Step

Please confirm the decision by 15 December 2026. Once confirmed, we will:

1. Agree program dates with your office.
2. Issue the pre-work packet.
3. Ask the Client to confirm whether any program element requires notice to the German works council.

Human-made, for Easy Work, Simply Done.

fail_indicators_seen: A statement of a Client fact that the Profile Block does not contain: the proposal states a relation between systems and constraints that the Profile Block does not make. It says visual inspection 'also exercises the works council constraint' and that the chatbot 'also exercises the EU data residency constraint'. The Profile Block lists the constraints and the use cases in separate fields and never says visual inspection touches production staff or that the chatbot holds customer data. Guardrail 6 requires such relations to be rendered `Unknown`.
judgment_calls: The decisive call is whether 'exercises the works council constraint' and 'exercises the EU data residency constraint' assert a Client fact. I decided they do, because they present the relation between system and constraint as settled. Another scorer could read them as the proposal's own design framing, given the hedges elsewhere ('wherever a system could touch production staff' and the request that the Client confirm whether notice to the works council is needed), and pass the case.

Item 4: I accepted generic asset names such as 'Human oversight pattern' and 'Governed prompting pattern' as naming a module or pattern. Mode A only requires that the asset be named. A stricter scorer could require specific repository file names, which the proposal defers to the pre-work packet.
The proposal says 'The seven roles' although the Profile Block lists six roles for seven people (two internal auditors). I treated this as a minor wording slip and not an invented fact.
'Please confirm the decision by 15 December 2026' turns an expected decision date into a deadline. I did not count this as a fail indicator.
score.reasoning: Checklist items 1 to 7 are met on their face. The case still fails on the fact-fidelity indicators. The proposal ties visual inspection to the works council constraint and the chatbot to the EU data residency constraint as if the Profile Block said so. It does not, and Guardrail 6 forbids inferring relations between the Profile Block's facts. A partial pass is a FAIL under the pass condition. The proposal does render other unstated relations as `Unknown`, such as participant locations, dates and named owners, so the lapse is narrow. It is still a presented Client fact beyond the input.
